content: SATI PRATHA
The Practice of Widow Immolation
A Historical & Sociological Overview
PART 1 — What Is It? An Introduction

Sati Pratha was a Hindu custom in which the widow of a dead man immolated herself willingly by sitting on her husband's funeral pyre. The practice of Sati in ancient times was voluntary, but during the medieval period, it was often forced on widows.
Source: Hinduism Facts

The term sati in Sanskrit means "good woman" or "chaste wife." Because that term was used in some instances to refer to a woman who ascended her deceased husband's funeral pyre, English usage of the term shifted to indicate the practice rather than the person. In ancient Sanskrit sources, the practice is called by terms referring to the action of ascending the funeral pyre, such as sahagamana ("going with"), anugamana ("going after"), sahamarana ("dying with"), and anumarana ("dying after"). In modern Hindi, the phrase sati pratha ("practice of sati") is used.
Source: Encyclopedia Britannica

The practice of sati is sometimes linked to the myth of the Hindu goddess Sati, who burns herself to death through her yogic powers after her father, Daksha, insulted her husband, the god Shiva. However, in this myth Shiva remains alive and avenges Sati's death. Hindu myths recount that Sati is then reincarnated as Shiva's wife Parvati.
Source: Encyclopedia Britannica

Sati Pratha, steeped in the historical traditions of India, once prevailed in certain communities where widowed women would immolate themselves on their husband's funeral pyre. This archaic ritual, though condemned by many, found justification among some Brahmin scholars and was perpetuated primarily among higher castes seeking to maintain social status.
Source: StudyIQ
The practice was, at its core, a convergence of religious belief, patriarchal control, economic motive, and psychological manipulation — all draped in the language of divine devotion.
PART 2 — Their Roots: Where Did It Come From?
Ancient Origins

According to historians, the Ramayana was written around 5 BCE and the Mahabharata around 3 BCE. The history of Sati Pratha dates back to at least 5 BCE. If we follow traditional Hindu views, it may date back to at least 10,000 BCE.
Source: Hinduism Facts

The first inscriptional evidence of the practice of sati was found in Nepal, as far back as 464 CE, according to scholar Axel Michaels. The Greeks mentioned Sati Pratha in their writing as early as 300 BCE. Initially confined to Rajput clans in western India, Sati Pratha became more widespread over time and traces its origins to ancient Hindu scriptures.
Source: Psychology Nepal
The Mythological Root

Sati is named after the Hindu goddess Sati, who is said to have burned herself to death after being humiliated by her father Daksha. The word 'sati' originally described the woman — meaning 'chaste woman' — and in Hindi and Sanskrit writings, the word is used interchangeably with 'good wife.'
Source: Reflections

Society considered Sati a loyal wife, and it was from here that the social practice got its name. After the incident, Lord Shiva went mad with grief, even trying to destroy the entire universe. Even after Sati came back as Parvati, Shiva did not easily accept her as his wife — showing how deeply he loved her. The irony? When we don't expect men to be as loving a husband as Shiva, why expect women to be a sacrificing wife as Sati?
Source: Eat My News
The Caste Connection
Sati Pratha was initially practiced mainly by some royal Kshatriya families, but later spread to other castes.
Source: Hinduism Facts

According to some scholars, Brahmins in northwest India adopted Rajput customs and changed the concept of sati from 'brave woman' to 'good woman.' Other non-warrior castes then adopted the practice once the Brahmins did. During the colonial era, the Sati practice surged again, especially in Bengal.
Source: Reflections
The Real Motivations Behind It
The practice was not purely spiritual. It was propped up by several darker, socio-economic reasons:
1. Religious Devotion (the stated reason)
Sati originated as a belief that immolating oneself on the husband's pyre demonstrated the highest level of devotion and loyalty to him.
Source: StudyIQ
2. Patriarchal Control

In ancient India, where patriarchal norms prevailed, Sati served to assert control over widows and enforce societal expectations. It also ensured that the husband's property remained intact within the family, avoiding disputes over inheritance.
Source: StudyIQ
3. Property and Greed

During the 1800s, the practice became prevalent in Bengal partly because Sati was forced by unscrupulous neighbors as a means of property annexation, and also due to poverty — since it was very hard for an alone widow to survive.
Source: Medium
4. Erasure of 'Inconvenient' Women

By eliminating widows through Sati, patriarchal systems effectively erased this 'problem,' ensuring both the preservation of family property and the maintenance of rigid gender hierarchies. The glorification of Sati reveals how patriarchy manipulated cultural and religious narratives to legitimize its dominance.
Source: ResearchGate
5. Fear of Widowhood
Some women may have chosen Sati to avoid the hardships and stigma associated with widowhood, seeking to maintain dignity and security.
Source: StudyIQ
It Was Not Unique to India
Many other cultures practiced similar rituals, including Greek, German, Slavic, Scandinavian, Egyptian, and Chinese societies — a fact often ignored in one-sided portrayals of this practice.
Source: Hinduism Facts
PART 3 — Fascinating (and Disturbing) Facts
🔥 Fact 1: The Practice Had a Dark Physical Reality

The actual practice of Sati was often brutal. Women who showed reluctance were often drugged or forcibly thrown onto the pyre. Many accounts describe instances of coercion and violence: women were often bound, gagged, or surrounded by men with sticks to prevent them from escaping the flames.
Source: Caste Free India

Emotional manipulation played a key role in convincing women to undergo Sati. They were told it was their duty to their husbands, their families, and their religion. They were promised eternal bliss in the afterlife and threatened with social ostracization if they refused.
Source: Caste Free India
🔢 Fact 2: The Numbers Were Staggering

Between 1815 and 1818, the number of documented Sati incidents in the Bengal Presidency doubled, from 378 to 839. Between 1815 and 1828, over 8,000 Sati cases were recorded in Bengal alone. In the year 1817 alone, about 700 widows were burnt alive.
Source: Wikipedia / BYJUS
👑 Fact 3: Kings' Wives Burned in Mass

When Raja Budh Singh died, his 84 wives became Sati. One of the wives of King Shivaji performed Sati 85 days after his death — her name was Putalabai. Interestingly, when Jijabai, the mother of Shivaji Maharaj, decided to go Sati after Shahaji Raje's death, Shivaji Maharaj personally prevented her from doing so.
Source: Hinduism Facts
🕌 Fact 4: Muslim Rulers Tried to Stop It — Long Before the British

Muhammad bin Tughlak was the first Muslim king who tried to stop Sati — he made it mandatory to obtain a license to burn the widow. Humayun prohibited the practice altogether but later retracted his order, fearing the wrath of God. Akbar tried to stop forced Sati cases, but did not interfere with those who willfully chose to burn themselves. He even offered gifts and land to widows to discourage them from performing Sati, and appointed men to prevent forced cases.
Source: Hinduism Facts
🇵🇹 Fact 5: The Portuguese Were First to Officially Ban It
The first formal ban on Sati was imposed by the Portuguese in Goa in 1515 — more than 300 years before the British did the same across India.
Source: GeeksforGeeks
👁️ Fact 6: A British Missionary Counted the Deaths

William Carey, a British Christian evangelist, noted 438 incidents of Sati within a 30-mile radius of Calcutta in 1803 alone, despite its ban within the city. He and his coworkers, known as the Serampore Trio, published essays forcefully condemning the practice and presented an address against Sati to the Governor-General.
Source: Wikipedia
🌅 Fact 7: It Was Banned — But Kept Happening

The British imposed the first formal ban on Sati in 1798, but only in Calcutta. Even after the ban, the practice continued in surrounding areas. There were 30 reported cases of Sati or attempted Sati over a 44-year period from 1943 to 1987 in India.
Source: Hinduism Facts / Wikipedia
💔 Fact 8: Raja Ram Mohan Roy — The Man Who Changed Everything

In 1812, Ram Mohan Roy began to champion the cause of banning Sati. He was motivated by witnessing his own sister-in-law being forced to die by Sati. He visited Kolkata's cremation grounds to personally persuade widows against immolation, formed watch groups to do the same, sought the support of elite Bengali classes, and wrote articles to show that Sati was not required by Hindu scripture.
Source: Wikipedia

In one of his works, Sambad Kaumudi, he proved there was no written proof to commit Sati in any Veda or epic. He argued it was entirely against women's right to live as human beings. In 1830, he even traveled to the United Kingdom as an ambassador of the Mughal Empire to ensure that Lord William Bentinck's Bengal Sati Regulation of 1829, banning Sati, was not overturned.
Source: GeeksforGeeks / Hinduism Facts
⚖️ Fact 9: The Abolition Law — December 4, 1829

The Bengal Sati Regulation, or Regulation XVII, A.D. 1829, made the practice of Sati illegal in all jurisdictions of British India, subject to legal prosecution. It was the first major social reform legislation enacted by the British in India, and it led to legislation against other old Hindu practices that limited women's rights. Rejecting a petition by 800 orthodox Hindus against the ban, the Privy Council upheld the ban on Sati in 1832.
Source: Wikipedia
😱 Fact 10: The Roop Kanwar Case — 1987, Not Ancient History

On September 4, 1987, Roop Kanwar, a Rajput woman in Deorala Village of Rajasthan, burned herself along with her dead husband on his funeral pyre. This incident was witnessed by thousands of people who did not try to prevent it. Roop Kanwar was 18 years old and had been married for just eight months to Maal Singh Shekhawat, who died suddenly due to an unknown illness.
Source: Hinduism Facts

She had tried to escape when she learned she would be burned to death, but was caught and forcibly taken to her husband's pyre. The Roop Kanwar case led to the enactment of the Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act in 1987, which made it illegal not only to commit or aid Sati, but also to glorify it — punishable by 1 to 7 years in prison.
Source: Worldwidejournals / GeeksforGeeks
🏛️ Fact 11: You Can Go to Jail Just for Praising It Today

Under India's current law, the Prevention of Sati Act makes it illegal to support, glorify, or attempt to die by Sati. Support of Sati, including coercing or forcing someone into it, can be punished by death penalty or life imprisonment, while glorifying Sati is punishable with one to seven years in prison.
Source: Wikipedia
🧠 Fact 12: The Widowhood Was Already a Punishment

Widows, often married as children to much older men, faced bleak futures even if they survived: shaved heads, white saris, and complete social ostracization. Sati was reframed as a 'sacred duty,' but many accounts describe women being drugged or bound to the pyre to prevent escape.
Source: Vocal Media
🌐 Fact 13: Jauhar — The Mass Version of Sati

Jauhar was a Hindu (Rajput) practice of mass self-immolation by women — or otherwise execution by their husbands, fathers, or brothers — in India, to avoid capture, enslavement, and rape by an invading army when facing defeat during war. Unlike Sati (mostly a single woman), Jauhar involved many Rajput women jumping into burning pyres when they were certain their husbands had lost in battle.
Source: Hinduism Facts
📅 Fact 14: The Last Known Reported Case Was in 2002
The last incident involving Sati, involving a 65-year-old woman, took place in Madhya Pradesh in 2002 — more than 170 years after the official ban.
Source: BYJUS
